hints: Focus on what a chiral centre really needs, a carbon with four single bonds to four different groups.
Look at the long chain first, every carbon there is either part of a C=C double bond or a $CH_2OH$ group.
Now check the six-membered ring for any $sp^3$ carbon with four different attachments, and see why the dimethyl carbon and the $CH_2$ groups fail the test.
walkthrough:
**Recall the test for chirality**

A chiral centre is an $sp^3$ carbon with four different groups attached. It must have four single bonds and no double bond, and no two identical substituents.

Rule to apply:
$$\text{chiral C} = \text{C with 4 single bonds to 4 different atoms/groups}$$

**Check the side chain**

The long chain is full of alternating C=C double bonds. Any carbon in a double bond has only three groups, so it cannot be chiral.

The only $sp^3$ carbon in the chain is the $-CH_2OH$ carbon, but it has two H atoms:
$$-CH_2-OH$$

**Check the six-membered ring**

Two ring carbons are part of a C=C double bond, so they are out. The carbon bearing two $CH_3$ groups has two identical methyl groups, so it is out.

The other three ring carbons are all $CH_2$ groups, each with two identical H atoms, so they are out too.

**Count and conclude**

No carbon in the whole molecule has four different single-bonded groups. Therefore the number of chiral centres is zero.

options.A: Correct. Every carbon is either $sp^2$ in a C=C bond, or $sp^3$ but with repeated groups such as two H atoms or two $CH_3$ groups. No carbon meets the four different single bonds test, so there are 0 chiral centres.
options.B: Incorrect. Students often pick the carbon with two methyl groups on the ring, thinking branching means chirality. It has two identical $CH_3$ groups, so it has only three different types of attachment and is achiral.
options.C: Incorrect. This suggests counting the ring junction carbons or $CH_2$ groups as chiral. All $CH_2$ groups have two identical H atoms, and the alkene carbons have only three attachments, so neither can be chiral.
options.D: Incorrect. This comes from confusing stereoisomerism around C=C (E/Z isomerism) with chiral centres. Vitamin A has many double bonds that show cis-trans isomerism, but a double-bonded carbon is never a chiral centre.
